title: Young people are using AI companions inside a shrinking relationship field while still preferring trusted human presence
source_unit: Young Life Research and Practice / Pinkston, RELATE Project 2026
geography: 11 countries: United States, United Kingdom, Argentina, Mexico, Hong Kong, India, Ethiopia, Kenya, Liberia, Nigeria, and Zimbabwe

observations.period: 2026; adolescents and young adults' AI-companion use and relationship preferences

denominator.unit: adolescents and young adults ages 13-24 surveyed across 11 countries

ai_use.unit: percent using AI in some way

ai_companion.unit: percent reporting an AI companion; 45% among ages 13-15 according to the publisher's summary

comfort.unit: percent of those with an AI companion saying they are more comfortable with it than with some friends or family

stress_and_advice.value: 12% say they cope with stress by talking to an AI companion and nearly 10% would turn to AI first for difficult advice

human_preference.value: 64% prefer connecting with close friends in person, up from 54% in the publisher's 2024 comparison; 70% prefer a trusted person over AI or online search for difficult advice

paradox.value: AI is functioning as an accessible, nonjudgmental substitute or bridge when human attention and confidentiality are scarce, while face-to-face trust remains the preferred endpoint

observations.method: RELATE Project 2026 survey summary and Young Life research blog; the publisher states the study covered 7,105 people ages 13-24 in 11 countries. The AI-companion and preference figures are publisher-reported survey results, not platform telemetry or a longitudinal causal test.
observations.uncertainty: The public materials do not provide a full questionnaire, weighting plan, response rates, recruitment frame, or complete subgroup denominators on the summary pages. Young Life is a faith-based nonprofit and the study's mission and interpretation may shape question selection, framing, and emphasis.
observations.subgroup: Adolescents and young adults ages 13-24, with particular attention to Gen Alpha ages 13-15, young people with limited adult listening support, and users of AI companions.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI companions may supplement rather than replace human relationships, and stated face-to-face preference may coexist with practical barriers such as distance, cost, stigma, time, or lack of safe trusted adults.

denominator.unit: RELATE Project 2026 participants ages 13-24 across 11 countries

confidentiality.unit: percent saying it is extremely or very important that someone keeps what they say private

adult_listening_gap.value: four in ten are not fully confident they have an adult in their life who is genuinely interested in listening

close_relationship_count.value: average reported close relationships declined from 5.3 in the 2024 comparison to 4.4 in the 2026 summary

trust_route.value: privacy, sustained attention, and being listened to are treated as scarce relationship infrastructure; AI can imitate availability but cannot establish reciprocal human commitment

observations.method: RELATE 2026 official project pages and executive-summary findings; the close-group count and listening-gap measures are publisher summaries, while the public pages do not expose the full item wording or variance.
observations.uncertainty: The comparison with 2024 may involve different samples, fieldwork, or question contexts; an average relationship count does not measure relationship quality, reciprocity, safety, or actual support. No causal effect of AI use or relationship decline is established.
observations.subgroup: Young people seeking confidential listening, trusted adults, peer connection, mentorship, and belonging across the 11-country study frame.
observations.counterinterpretation: A smaller reported close circle may represent more selective or digitally distributed relationships rather than a uniform collapse in meaningful support; confidentiality preferences can also reflect ordinary developmental boundary-setting.

observations.period: 2026; qualitative explanation of AI companionship and human connection

denominator.unit: Gen Z and Gen Alpha voices in 22 RELATE 2.0 focus groups across 11 countries

qualitative_route.value: participants describe AI as patient, available, and less judgmental, while describing human presence, mentorship, and real-world conversation as more authentic and relationally consequential

formation_question.value: the emerging issue is not only whether young people use AI, but whether AI-mediated reassurance changes help-seeking, privacy expectations, adult mentorship, emotional vocabulary, and offline participation

next_test.value: follow a named youth-serving setting or cohort through AI use, adult listening access, confidentiality, advice quality, referral or escalation, offline participation, and later wellbeing

observations.method: RELATE 2026 resources page reporting 22 focus groups and 97 Gen Z/Alpha voices; quotations are illustrative qualitative evidence and are not prevalence estimates.
observations.uncertainty: Focus-group participants and selected quotations may not represent the broader survey sample or all young people; the publisher's faith-based mission may shape recruitment, interpretation, and the proposed adult-support response.
observations.subgroup: Young people in the focus groups, adult mentors, parents, educators, faith leaders, youth organizations, and designers of AI companion systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Young people may use AI for low-stakes experimentation while reserving meaningful trust for humans; the distinction between companion, tool, search, and entertainment may be fluid across contexts.

related_sources.claim: Official study description with the 7,105-person, 11-country sample and country counts.
Official resources page with the executive summary, focus-group description, and qualitative themes.
Meta-Gallup global social-connection evidence provides a broader, non-ministry comparative context.

boundary: This record adds a youth relationship-and-AI companionship route from shrinking or insufficient human listening capacity through AI use, confidentiality, advice, face-to-face preference, mentorship, and offline connection. It is publisher-reported survey and qualitative evidence from a faith-based nonprofit, not independent population surveillance, platform telemetry, causal evidence, mental-health diagnosis, or proof that AI companions replace human relationships.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official RELATE home, about, resources, and Young Life blog pages were reviewed for sample size, countries, AI-companion shares, face-to-face and trusted-person preferences, confidentiality, listening gap, relationship-count comparison, and focus-group scope.
